articles.title: Smashing Security podcast #488: How a ransomware negotiator ended up arrested at his own conference
articles.summary:
A ransomware negotiator attended a cybersecurity conference, only to be arrested by the FBI in connection with its investigation into the ShinyHunters gang.

Meanwhile, hackers get the keys to ASOS's app and the chance to message every single customer. What did they say? And how did the company respond? We have thoughts.

All this and more is discussed in episode 488 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Paul Ducklin.

articles.title: Weekly Update 525: AI Data Breach Hyperbole
articles.summary: I remember the name of that AI doco now - The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist. I was watching it on the long-haul flight home the other day, and what I found particularly engrossing was the polar-opposite opinions from a bunch of people: "it'
articles.full_text: I remember the name of that AI doco now - The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist. I was watching it on the long-haul flight home the other day, and what I found particularly engrossing was the polar-opposite opinions from a bunch of people: "it's gonna kill us all" versus "it's gonna make us all rich", and so on. But to some extent, I can understand the gap between opinions when we're all just speculating about the future. I have much less understanding for why people infatuate with hyping AI as a data breach monster when the evidence to date is quite the opposite. In fact, I've enjoyed sharing example after example of recent breaches perpetrated by kids with a telephone (vishing), while pointing out I haven't seen a single one orchestrated by AI.Speaking of AI, a big thanks to this week's sponsor who's doing gtreat things in the agent observability space, Origin. The machines may not be dumping data that lands in HIBP (yet), but they do go off-script and Origin will help trace back precisely what happened when it all goes wrong.

articles.title: GTA 6 leaker threatens to release full playable version of game ahead of official launch
articles.summary:
The hacker behind a high-profile string of leaks involving the upcoming release of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 videogame has threatened to release a complete, playable build.


Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.
articles.full_text:
The hacker behind a high-profile string of leaks involving the upcoming release of the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 videogame has threatened to release a complete, playable build.
The website of "CyberLeek" published the threat shortly after releasing around 25 minutes of fresh footage of the blockbuster game due to be released in November by Rockstar Games.
Eurogamer, which has seen the footage, says it appears to be legitimate, and confirmed that it carries the emblem of CyberLeek.
According to CyberLeek, the full playable build of GTA 6 will be released when its own cryptocurrency coin reaches a market cap of US $30 million. In an attempt to give its claims more credence, CyberLeek says that any doubters can request specific scenes to confirm it has access to the entire game.
CyberLeek says that if the GTA 6 game is released on physical disk, and a public apology is made, it will step back from its threats.
Campaign groups like Stop Killing Games which fights games to remain playable after publishers end support, have reportedly distanced themselves from CyberLeek's actions, and in August posted on Reddit that gamers should not encourage CyberLeek:
"Do not send these people your money, no matter how much sympathy you may feel for their actions. This is illegal, and frankly, we feel for everyone at Rockstar having to go through this ordeal again, especially just over a week before Rockstar’s own official “Extended Look” premieres."
Take-Two, Rockstar’s parent company, appears to be hell bent on identifying whoever is behind the leaks, and has attempted to subpoena Microsoft and Discord in order to gather information about their possible identity.
Anyone who works in the field of cybersecurity is too familiar with the refrain of "pay up or we release it." What is unusual in this case is that the hacker in not demanding a direct ransom payment, but is instead asking their audience to pump up the value of a crypto token. The hacker's hope is that the pent-up desire of enough Grand Theft Auto fans will boost how much the crypto coins are worth.
But, of course, there is no guarantee that the hackers will release a full, playable version of the game - even if their cryptocurrency coin does reach US $30 million.
As ever, videogame fans should be very wary of believing anybody who offers a download of a supposedly leaked game. Especially when a game is as hyped-up as GTA 6, there is a real risk that unsuspecting fans will be duped into making bad decisions that could put their computer security at risk.
Besides which, the real, genuine GTA 6 is due to be released on video game platforms on 19 November. It is not worth infecting your computer, or losing money on a dodgy crypto coin, just to see it a few weeks early.

articles.full_text:
When evaluating media provenance, the single most critical requirement is having consistent and repeatable results.

Imagine evidence presented in a courtroom: the prosecution presents a validation report claiming an image is real, while the defense presents a different validator showing it is fake. What is the jury supposed to think? If a judge admits both reports under Frye, Daubert, or Kumho standards, then the jury isn't just judging the media. The jury is forced to decide which software implementation to trust, undermining the goal of automated digital provenance. (Disclaimer: I am not an attorney and this is not a legal interpretation.)

Not every provenance validation solution is intended for legal use. Setting legal standards aside, consider the business implications. Companies often rely on partially-vetted heuristics to make important decisions. As an organization making critical decisions, would you rely on a solution that is designed to return contradictory findings? The wrong decision can result in customer complaints and damage your corporate reputation.

We could even consider a lower standard: social media. It's common to have online arguments and flame wars around contradicting opinions. However, when each side is backed by their own validation approach, it ends up increasing the divide rather than enabling a consensus.

This is the reality that has been provided to us from the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). They have released a provenance solution that enables contradicting results. Moreover, they have backed it with a massive media blitz and widespread tech adoption.

Required Validation
In my previous blog entry, I walked through how different provenance solutions handle their verification workflows. Transport Layer Security (TLS, used by HTTPS) uses a strict, deterministic validation process (with only a small variation based on trust lists). Secure Evidence Attribution Label (SEAL) is only slightly more complex and has less variation. As long as you implement either protocol correctly, every validator should reach the exact same conclusion every single time.

C2PA takes the opposite approach. Its specifications rely on a complex workflow with explicit "optional" steps. Because these checks are optional, two fully spec-compliant validators can evaluate the exact same file and arrive at conflicting results. Moreover, users may never know which options the validator used.

(Click to see larger.)
 

In this workflow diagram, every red decision box highlights a step where optional parameters allow validators to diverge and produce conflicting outputs. The main issues are around which trust list is used (workflow steps 2 and 6), whether revocation is checked (steps 3, 7, 9, and 10), and how the timestamp is validated (steps 6, 7, and 9). This ambiguity-by-design in C2PA's workflow leads to two specific problems:
The specifications permit differences in validation behavior. This cannot be blamed on coding errors. Two validators can function properly and be fully compliant, and still reach conflicting results based on which options they choose to implement.

These differences can cause materially misleading conclusions about a file's trustworthiness. Users cannot reliably determine whether a file is authentic, AI-generated, edited, or trustworthy based on a validator's assessment. Even if every validator you test reaches the same conclusion, there could always be another validator that comes up with a different result.
Showing a workflow and claiming that a specification enables contradictory results is one thing, but proving it with real-world data is another. Throughout this post, I will walk through actual image files to demonstrate how C2PA's validation workflow breaks down in practice at each step.

Testing Methodology
To keep the comparison fair and comprehensive, I evaluated test images across a range of C2PA validators:
Adobe Content Authenticity Inspect (https://contentauthenticity.adobe.com/inspect) is a "conforming product", which means that the implementation's details have been reviewed by C2PA and vetted against the specs.

Verifieddit (verifieddit.com) from SanMarcSoft LLC is another conforming validator.

CAI Verify (verify.contentauthenticity.org) is built and maintained directly by Adobe's Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) using their official open-source JavaScript SDK. Ironically, despite being widely cited across CAI and C2PA publications, sharing development teams with Adobe Inspect (a conforming product), and using versions of the same JavaScript SDK, CAI Verify is not listed as a conforming product.

IPTC Origin Verify (originverify.iptc.org) is provided by the International Press Telecommunication Council.

C2PA.sh is provided by SSL.com, a commercial Certificate Authority and C2PA Trusted CA.

Proofmode Verify (formerly "ProofCheck", check.proofmode.org) is provided by Proofmode, an early adopter of C2PA. Today, they have conforming generators for Android and iOS, but they are not listed as a conforming validator.

Sony has a signature self checker that recognizes Sony's own C2PA signatures.
Along with the validators, I also used a wide range of pictures. Each picture is included in this blog. At any time, you can click on the picture to see the full-size file, save the file to your computer, and then upload it to any of these validators. (Don't take my word for it! Verify my findings and claims!)

While each of these platforms implement C2PA's solution, their outputs frequently disagree. Here is how that plays out in practice.

Although the C2PA specifications recommend how the user interface should report results, few tools follow those recommendations. Also keep in mind, everything with C2PA is dynamic. I did this test on 2026-10-12. If I did this same test 3 months ago, the results would have included a few different inconsistencies. (I'm sure that these vendors will see these results, make more changes without any coordination, and cause more contradictions.)

Example: Nikon and The Flying Pug
Click on the image to see the full size picture and save it for uploading to the validators.

 

This picture has a well-known history. In September 2025 (over a year ago), Nikon released C2PA for their Z6 III camera. Within days, researcher Adam Horshack figured out how to use this to sign any picture as if it came from the Nikon Z6 III. DP Review published details about the vulnerability. Literally the next day Nikon disabled their C2PA signing service, and they revoked their signing cert two weeks later.

If the validator checks for revocation, then it will report that the cert has been revoked. For example, c2pa.sh says that the image is "UNTRUSTED" because the certificate was revoked.

 

Unfortunately, as seen in the workflow, checking for revocation is optional. Neither conforming product (Verifieddit and Adobe Inspect) checks for revocation, so they report that the content is "Trusted". In fact, Verifieddit even adds, "The signature checks out and the source is one we recognise, so this photo appears to be a real, unedited capture."

 

Adobe Inspect has no banners or warnings about the picture being untrusted. At best, it has a small note that this picture from 2025 uses a "legacy version" of C2PA.

 

IPTC provides the only validator that says it checks multiple trust lists. They have teeny tiny icons with teeny tiny alert icons and on-hover text to identify which trust lists match the signature. Ignoring the poor usability aspect, identifying which trust list matched is a cool feature.

 

With the flying pug picture, first and third icons have tiny orange "!" symbols, indicating that the signature is not on the IPTC or C2PA trust lists. The second icon (a black-and-white squiggle box) has no tiny orange "!", indicating that it matched the ITL. IPTC also reports that there is no timestamp, even though Adobe Inspect shows a timestamp.

The CAI-managed Interim Trust List (ITL) was created as a temporary solution before C2PA had an official trust list. The ITL was official

articles.full_text:
Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms:
Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work.
There are a lot of caveats to this analysis. It relies on published work, so anything unpublished does not count. This includes both academic cryptanalysis that didn’t result in a paper, and intelligence agency cryptanalysis done in secret. But it’s a good first stab at a metric of this sort.

articles.title: The Future of AI Cryptanalysis
articles.summary:
Matthew Green has been writing a rather pessimistic series of posts about the potential for AI systems to vastly outperform humans in cryptanalysis of both symmetric and public-key ciphers.
I am more optimistic than he is. That is, I have stronger faith in the over-engineering cryptographers tend to do. I am trying to write this up in more detail.

articles.full_text:
Another IoT cyberattack, this one in France:
Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.
[…]
Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.
Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.
Any IoT device that can’t be updated is vulnerable. And, probably, any IoT device that can be updated is also vulnerable.
